content.body: Anagrams are words that contain the same letters in a different order. Today we'll learn how to efficiently check if two words are anagrams using a clever memory technique. This approach will help you solve many similar problems where you need to track what you've seen.
content.title: Introduction

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:
1. Explain why checking letter counts is better than sorting
2. Implement a character frequency counter using an object
3. Determine when two words are valid anagrams
4. Apply the 'remember what we've seen' approach to similar problems
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's start with a simple example. Are these two words anagrams?
content.title: Try it
content.successMessage: Good! Both words contain the same letters: c, a, t.

content.title: Try a longer word
content.successMessage: Correct! Both have the same letters: l, i, s, t, e, n.

content.title: One more
content.successMessage: Right! They don't share the same letters, so they're not anagrams.

content.body: You mentally compared the letters in each word. For short words, this works well, but for longer words or when comparing many pairs, we need a systematic approach.
content.title: What you did

content.body: Imagine checking if two 10,000-character strings are anagrams. Manually comparing letters becomes impossible. We need a method that works efficiently regardless of length. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: The core idea is to remember what we've already seen. Instead of comparing letters directly, we'll count how many times each letter appears in both words. If the counts match for all letters, the words are anagrams.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it like a notebook where we write down each letter we see and how many times it appears. Then we compare notebooks to see if they match.

content.body: We'll use a lookup structure (like an object) to store letter counts. For each word, we'll count its letters, then compare the counts.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
Example with 'cat' and 'act':
1. Count letters in 'cat': c:1, a:1, t:1
2. Count letters in 'act': a:1, c:1, t:1
3. Compare counts: they match exactly!
4. Conclusion: valid anagrams.

content.body:
1. If the words have different lengths, they can't be anagrams
2. Create an object to store letter frequencies
3. Count letters in the first word (add to counts)
4. Count letters in the second word (subtract from counts)
5. If all counts are zero at the end, they're anagrams
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Check lengths
steps.instruction: First, let's handle the simple case: if the words have different lengths, they can't be anagrams. Add this check at the beginning of the function.
steps.hint: Use the .length property on both strings and compare them.
steps.expectedOutcome: Return false immediately if lengths differ
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Different lengths mean different letter counts, so they can't be anagrams.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Remember to return false if the lengths don't match.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try comparing s.length and t.length. If they're different, return false.

steps.title: Create frequency counter
steps.instruction: Now create an object to store letter frequencies. We'll use this to remember what we've seen.
steps.hint: Initialize an empty object using {} or new Object().
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! This object will help us track letter counts.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. You need to declare a variable to hold the frequency object.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try creating an empty object, like: const freq = {};

steps.title: Count letters in first word
steps.instruction: Loop through the first word and count each letter. Add 1 to the frequency count for each letter.
steps.hint: Use a for loop or for...of to iterate through the string. For each character, increment its count in the freq object.
steps.expectedOutcome: The freq object contains counts for all letters in s
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! Now we're remembering what we've seen in the first word.
steps.feedbackPartial: You need to iterate through each character of s and update the freq object.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: for (let char of s) { freq[char] = (freq[char] || 0) + 1; }

steps.title: Count letters in second word
steps.instruction: Now loop through the second word. This time, subtract 1 from the frequency count for each letter.
steps.hint: Use a similar loop for t. For each character, decrement its count in the freq object.
steps.expectedOutcome: The freq object now has net counts (positive for extra letters in s, negative for extra in t)
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! If the words are anagrams, all counts should be zero after this step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Remember to iterate through t and subtract from the frequency counts.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: for (let char of t) { freq[char] = (freq[char] || 0) - 1; }

steps.title: Check all counts are zero
steps.instruction: Finally, check if all values in the frequency object are zero. If any value is non-zero, the words aren't anagrams.
steps.hint: Use Object.values() to get all counts, then check if every value equals 0.
steps.expectedOutcome: Return true if all counts are zero, false otherwise
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You've implemented the complete anagram checker.
steps.feedbackPartial: You need to check every value in the freq object and return the appropriate boolean.

content.body:
Great work! You've learned how to use a frequency counter to check if two words are anagrams. Remember:
1. The key insight is to remember what we've seen using a lookup structure
2. We store letters as keys and counts as values
3. We check the structure as we process the second word
4. This approach works efficiently for any length string

This 'remember what we've seen' pattern applies to many problems where you need to track frequencies or check for matches.
content.title: Done
